posts.title: Thanksgiving
posts.description: In her essay, "Open Wide Thy Hand," Marilynne Robinson considers the origins of American liberalism and its particular dependence on the writings of Moses in the Hebrew Bible. She argues that American liberalism is the child of Calvinism and, in particular, Calvinism's close reading of the Old Testament. I cite Robinson today because I think she offers us a refreshing and interesting way of reframing the place of Christianity in our nation's public life. In a common framing of contemporary political disputes, the question of Christian presence in American public life is framed in stark and alarming terms, as if it is a question of how one feels about some imaginative work of dystopian fiction, such as The Handmaid's Tale . In the past, this line of attack was mostly a slur, a kind of red scare type tactic deployed by progressives and various New Atheist writers against relatively conventional Christian conservatives. posts.title: Greedy, Dragonish Thoughts
posts.description: One of the most memorable moments in C. S. Lewis’ beloved Chronicles of Narnia series is the adventure of Eustace with the dragon and his lair on what Caspian later names Dragon Island. Readers, both children and adults alike, remember this adventure because it is the moment of redemption: an encounter with Aslan begins changing the selfish, obtuse, and annoying Eustace into a boy of compassion, courage, and sacrifice. In The Voyage of the Dawn Treader , Lewis depends on dragon imagery and symbolism from both Scripture and the Medieval world of which Lewis was a scholar. In Scripture, the dragon most notably represents the Devil. The dragon is a fitting image of the one who both invades the garden of Eden in the form of a serpent, and who also “prowls around like a roaring lion looking for someone to devour.” Imagery of serpents and leviathan all are related to dragons and thus to the devil. posts.title: Reading Musculus on the 23rd Psalm
posts.description: One of the things I'm most excited about with the launch of The Faith Received is the chance to dive into authors I've been aware of for some time, but have not been able to read since I do not know Latin. Given my phase of life (four kids, two elementary age and two middle school) and professional obligations, I have no prospects of learning it in the near future just due to lack of time. But thanks to Ian and Stiven's work, I can now read many of these thinkers. So in the months to come I will be writing some short notes based on my time spent in TFR. I hope others will contribute to this as well. Today I want to draw out three things from Wolfgang Musculus's commentary on Psalm 23. Musculus has long been of interest to me for some time because he is a contemporary of the first generation of reformers.
